[ASSISTANT_SAID] Antique door knockers from the Victorian era (1837-1901) are treasured collectibles.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Factors that make Victorian door knockers valuable include rarity, materials, craftsmanship, historical significance, condition, uniqueness, and provenance.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Where to find Victorian door knockers within budget includes estate sales and auctions, antique dealers and shops, online marketplaces, flea markets and antique fairs, and restoration and salvage yards.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Budget-friendly options for door knockers range from $100-$500 for simple, smaller pieces to $5,000-$10,000 for rare, unique, or highly ornate pieces.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Tips for buying include researching, inspecting carefully, negotiating, considering restoration, and getting documentation.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Antique restoration classes can be hands-on workshops, lecture-based classes, or combination classes.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Typical class duration can range from a few hours to several days or weeks, with small class sizes of 5-15 students.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Skills learned in antique restoration classes include assessment and evaluation, cleaning and stabilizing, finishing techniques, repair and conservation, materials identification, historical context, safety protocols, and troubleshooting.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Where to find antique restoration classes includes local colleges and universities, professional organizations, online platforms, specialized schools, and private instructors.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Recommended online resources for furniture restoration include The Furniture Restoration Institute, Furniture Restoration School, The Wood Whisperer, Udemy, Craftsy, and various online communities and forums.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Suggested YouTube channels for furniture restoration include The Furniture Restoration Channel, Furniture Fixer Upper, and Woodworking Adventures.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Recommended books for furniture restoration include "Furniture Restoration: A Comprehensive Guide" by Fred Taylor, "The Furniture Bible" by Christophe Pourny, and "The Restoration of Antique Furniture" by John Kelsey.
